overview.title: 📖 Overview: From the Decapitated Heifer to the Guilt Offering of the Pious
overview.subtitle: Keritot 25a–25b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues the dispute over when the prohibition on benefiting from a decapitated heifer (eglah arufah) begins, with Rav Hamnuna and Rava trading proofs from parallel mishnayot and adjusting the text to defend their positions, before the Gemara settles the matter as a genuine tannaitic dispute. A new mishna then introduces one of the more striking figures in the tractate: Bava ben Buta, who — following Rabbi Eliezer's view that a provisional guilt offering may be brought voluntarily — sacrificed one every single day except the day after Yom Kippur. This launches a debate over whether such an offering can ever be a true gift, or whether, as the Rabbis hold, it is always fundamentally obligatory. The daf closes by tracing, through several rounds of proposed verses and objections, exactly why Yom Kippur atones for uncertain sins (exempting one from ever bringing a provisional guilt offering after the day passes) while it does not atone for confirmed sins requiring a sin or guilt offering.

slides.title: 🐄 When Does the Heifer Actually Become Forbidden?
slides.subtitle: Rav Hamnuna and Rava trade proofs and text-adjustments

lines.speaker: Rav Hamnuna
lines.text: Proof from Ḥullin: Rabbi Shimon exempts one who slaughters the heifer (rather than decapitating it) from the 'mother and offspring' prohibition, because he holds 'slaughter that doesn't render fit for consumption isn't real slaughter' — meaning the heifer was ALREADY forbidden from benefit while alive!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Proof from OUR mishna: it says discovering innocence BEFORE decapitation lets the heifer simply 'go graze with the flock' — implying no prohibition existed yet while alive!

lines.speaker: Counter-adjustment
lines.text: Reread the mishna as 'before it became FIT for decapitation' (i.e., before reaching the valley) — consistent with my view that once fit, even while alive, it's forbidden.

lines.speaker: Further proof
lines.text: But the mishna's own reasoning says the heifer 'atones for its uncertainty' only once decapitated — while alive, no atonement has occurred, so no prohibition should apply yet either!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: This is a genuine dispute between tanna'im — a baraita comparing the heifer to other 'enabling' offerings outside the Temple confirms Rav Hamnuna's position, that prohibition begins from life itself.

callout.label: Rava's silence:
callout.text: When first challenged, Rava had no answer and stayed silent — only later realizing he could have argued Rabbi Shimon holds the heifer IS validly killed by slaughter, contradicting a different mishna's assumption.

slides.title: 🙏 Bava ben Buta's Daily Offering
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: Rabbi Eliezer's view that anyone may bring a provisional guilt offering purely voluntarily
rows: A person may volunteer a provisional guilt offering any day, at any time — called 'the guilt offering of the pious' (אֲשַׁם חֲסִידִים)
Brought one every single day — except the day immediately after Yom Kippur
He swore he would have brought one even that day too, if permitted
Told to 'wait until you enter a situation of potential uncertainty' — some real doubt must exist first, even if minor
A provisional guilt offering may be brought ONLY for uncertainty about a sin that would carry karet if intentional and a sin offering if unwitting

callout.label: Practical framing:
callout.text: Even according to those who permitted Bava ben Buta's near-daily practice, some minimal genuine uncertainty was still required — pure invention was never sanctioned.

slides.title: 🎁 Gift or Obligation?
slides.subtitle: Is a provisional guilt offering ever truly voluntary — and does it fully atone?

lines.speaker: Gemara's proof for Rabbi Eliezer
lines.text: If it were purely obligatory, why would someone who brought one still need a SIN offering once his sin becomes certain? He'd already have fulfilled his obligation! Since he doesn't, the guilt offering must be voluntary.

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: Burnt and peace offerings can be voluntary, but sin and guilt offerings — including the provisional one — are always obligatory. One brings it beforehand purely to spare the person needless suffering while awaiting clarity, not as a true 'gift.'

lines.speaker: A challenging baraita
lines.text: 'Five guilt offerings achieve complete atonement; the provisional guilt offering does not achieve complete atonement' — meaning if the sin later proves definite, ANOTHER offering is still required.

lines.speaker: Ravina's reading
lines.text: Alternative: the five REQUIRE nothing else once brought; the provisional guilt offering's uncertainty is resolved by something ELSE entirely — namely, Yom Kippur itself, since if the year ends before certainty arrives, no sin offering is ever needed at all.

callout.label: Underlying stakes:
callout.text: Whether the provisional guilt offering is a gift or an obligation shapes whether Rabbi Eliezer's daily practice reflects genuine piety or a technical loophole.

slides.title: 🗓️ Does Yom Kippur Atone for Known Sins?
slides.subtitle: Tracing why sin/guilt-offering-level sins still require their offering even after Yom Kippur

nodes.content: ❓ Why does the mishna say those liable to sin/guilt offerings must STILL bring them after Yom Kippur passes, while provisional-guilt-offering cases are exempt?

📜 Rav Dimi (R' Ami/R' Ḥanina): Lev. 16:16 equates 'sins' with 'transgressions' — just as the scapegoat atones for INTENTIONAL transgressions (which carry no offering), it atones for unwitting sins only when THEY too carry no offering

🛑 Abaye's objection: that verse discusses the INSIDE goat, which never atones for known violations at all — maybe the SCAPEGOAT (which does atone for known violations) atones for everything, offering-eligible or not!

🔄 Abaye redirects to Lev. 16:21 (the scapegoat's own confession verse) for the same 'sins like transgressions' comparison — but Rav Dimi challenges: how do we know 'transgressions' here even excludes offering-eligible sins? (four cases bring offerings even for INTENTIONAL violation!)

✅ Final resolution: the verse's own structure — 'iniquities' (intentional) THEN 'transgressions and ALL their sins' — teaches by extra emphasis that sins parallel to non-offering transgressions are what's atoned, excluding sins that DO carry an offering

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: Yom Kippur's atonement is broad but not unlimited — it reaches purely 'between a person and God' sins, not sins the Torah has already assigned a specific offering to resolve.

slides.title: 🤫 A Sin Only God Knows
slides.subtitle: Why the provisional guilt offering specifically becomes unnecessary once Yom Kippur passes
slides.label: The derivation:
slides.text: Rabbi Elazar locates the source in Leviticus 16:30: 'For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be pure before the Lord.' The phrase 'before the Lord' signals a sin known only to God — precisely the character of an uncertain transgression that would otherwise require a provisional guilt offering. Since no human being (including the sinner himself) can confirm whether it occurred, Yom Kippur's atonement reaches it completely, closing the matter without further sacrifice. Rav Taḥlifa (in Rava's name) notes this reasoning does not equally prove the mishna's parallel claim about definite sin and guilt offerings, which are governed by the separate derivation explored earlier in the daf.

summary.principle: Whether a prohibition on benefit begins at life or at a defining ritual act, whether an offering is truly voluntary or fundamentally obligatory, and how far Yom Kippur's atonement extends are all questions resolved through careful comparison of parallel verses and mishnayot — never assumed from a single surface reading.

flowSteps.content: 🐄 Rav Hamnuna and Rava dispute when the eglah arufah's prohibition begins, resolved as a genuine tannaitic disagreement
🙏 Bava ben Buta's near-daily provisional guilt offering illustrates Rabbi Eliezer's view that some uncertainty always suffices
🎁 The Rabbis insist even this offering is fundamentally obligatory, brought early only to spare needless suffering

columns.content: 🗓️ Yom Kippur's atonement is shown, through careful verse comparison, to exclude sins that carry their own specific offering
🤫 But it fully covers uncertain sins 'known only to God,' exempting the provisional guilt offering entirely

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the precise boundary of an atonement mechanism is drawn from the structure of its governing verses, distinguishing what it can and cannot resolve

quiz.q: According to Rav Hamnuna's proof from the mishna in Ḥullin, why does Rabbi Shimon exempt one who slaughters (rather than decapitates) the eglah arufah from the 'mother and offspring' prohibition?
o: Because the heifer is not really an animal
Because slaughter that doesn't render an item fit for consumption isn't considered slaughter, since the heifer was already forbidden from benefit from when it was alive
Because the mother-and-offspring prohibition never applies to heifers
Because Rabbi Shimon rejects the entire eglah arufah ritual
quiz.e: Rav Hamnuna explains that Rabbi Shimon's exemption only makes sense if the heifer was already forbidden from benefit while alive, making the slaughter act not a 'real' slaughter (since it can't render an already-forbidden animal fit for consumption).

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what did Bava ben Buta do every day except the day after Yom Kippur?
o: He fasted
He voluntarily brought a provisional guilt offering, following Rabbi Eliezer's view
He brought a sin offering
He studied Torah exclusively
quiz.e: Bava ben Buta, following Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that a provisional guilt offering may be brought voluntarily any day, brought one daily — except the day after Yom Kippur, since that day's atonement already covers any uncertain sin.

quiz.q: According to the Rabbis (as opposed to Rabbi Eliezer), why is a provisional guilt offering brought even before the underlying sin becomes certain?
o: Because it is a purely voluntary gift offering, like a burnt offering
Because it is fundamentally an obligatory offering, brought early specifically to spare the person from needless suffering while awaiting clarity
Because the Torah requires daily offerings from everyone
Because it has no connection to any actual sin
quiz.e: The Rabbis hold that a provisional guilt offering, unlike a burnt or peace offering, is always obligatory in nature; it is brought before certainty arrives only because the Torah spares people from prolonged anxiety, not because it is a discretionary gift.

quiz.q: According to Rav Dimi's initial derivation (via Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Ḥanina), what principle does Leviticus 16:16 teach about the scope of Yom Kippur's atonement?
o: That Yom Kippur atones for absolutely everything without exception

That 'sins' (unwitting violations) are compared to 'transgressions' (intentional violations) — Yom Kippur atones for unwitting sins only when they, like most intentional transgressions, are not subject to atonement through a specific offering
That Yom Kippur has no atoning power at all
That only priests can be atoned for on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: The derivation compares 'sins' to 'transgressions' in the verse, teaching that Yom Kippur's atonement for unwitting sins parallels its atonement for intentional transgressions — reaching only those not already assigned a specific offering by the Torah.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Elazar, what phrase in Leviticus 16:30 explains why one is exempt from ever bringing a provisional guilt offering once Yom Kippur has passed?
o: 'You shall afflict your souls'
'Before the Lord' — indicating a sin known only to God, exactly matching the character of an uncertain transgression
'In the seventh month'
'A statute forever'
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar derives from the phrase 'before the Lord' in Leviticus 16:30 that Yom Kippur atones for sins known only to God — precisely the uncertain sins that would otherwise require a provisional guilt offering, rendering it unnecessary after Yom Kippur passes.
